newsitem.title: USA: Latin American woes won't derail reform process say experts.
newsitem.headline: Latin American woes won't derail reform process say experts.

text.p: Growing labour unrest and a backlash against austerity measures in Latin America may slow the pace of economic reforms in the region but they won't derail the process, emerging market experts say.

"You may see some backsliding or slowing down of the reform process but if you look at the whole thing in context, no one is really going way back," said Susan Kaufman Purcell, vice president at the Council of the Americas.
Populist sounding rhetoric seem to be taking hold in countries throughout the region.

In Colombia, a massive nationwide strike protesting wage increases of 13.5 percent proposed by the government instead of the 21.5 percent wage increase requested by labour unions continued as talks with government ministers broke down.

And in Ecuador, a nationwide strike against increases in public sector tariffs and subsidy cuts, along with alleged government corruption, resulted in the removal last week of the country's president, Abdala Bucaram, on the grounds of mental incompetence.

"What the real problem is is that people in society feel that others are benefitting from reforms but they're not, and so at some point, depending on how much they are pressed, they will take to the streets," said Purcell.
Despite the recent backlash against tough government austerity measures and smaller-than-expected spending increases, emerging market experts believe market reforms, albeit slowly, will continue.

"The alternative to tough economic reforms is populism and that is a bankrupt idea in Latin America," said Thomas Trebat, managing director for emerging market research at Citicorp Securities in New York.
In the case of Ecuador, he explained that Bucaram was trying to do too much too fast.

"There can be bumps in the road; there can setbacks, and there can be revisions, but policy reforms in Latin America will continue wherever there is a strong social consensus behind them and that consensus exists in Ecuador to move slowly and to move gradually," Trebat said.
Sources said that even the populist agenda of Venezuelan President Rafael Caldera fell by the wayside after he tried to buck the tide by implementing foreign exchange controls and price controls.
Indeed, investors started to move capital back into Venezuela after Caldera reversed his stance.
Still, some experts warned that the next wave of reform in Latin America would be far more difficult.

"There has been a tremendous return to capital over the last six years throughout the globe and now it looks like labour wants its share of that chunk," said Gary Evans, senior emerging market debt strategist at Lehman Brothers.

Though the initial phase of reforms in countries such as Argentina and Brazil was extremely popular because it reduced hyperinflation and thus increased individual purchasing power, experts said the next stage would be more difficult because it will entail public sector layoffs and loss of benefits.
For example, they said labour reform in Argentina is likely to continue to meet widespread opposition given the country's near 18 percent unemployment rate.

"In the case of (Argentine President Carlos) Menem, he has little real room because of the 18 percent unemployment. The real issue is that it is going to be very hard to convince labour unions with 18 percent unemployment to give up any benefits," said Riordan Roett, head of the Latin American Studies Programme at Johns Hopkins University in Maryland.
Venezuela is another country where the the reform process may slow if lower-than-expected public sector wage increases result in labour strife.
At the same time, experts cautioned that Venezuela needs to be careful not to use windfall oil profits to pay for those public sector wage increases.
